utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if I could address you, please. Before we continue with the evidence, there is an outstanding application for provisional release, which we will deal with now, on behalf of Mr. Cerkez. The application can be dealt with briefly, but let me first mention something about tomorrow. I hope the message has reached all parties that we shall not be sitting tomorrow morning. That is because one of our number has to attend at a hospital appointment. We will resume at half past two tomorrow. We would normally sit until 5.30, but I think I may have a meeting at 5.00, but I'll have to confirm that. Turning to the application, is there anything you want to add to your written submissions, which we've seen? I can perhaps add this before you do. We have obviously considered this matter while we've been away, and we're of the view that potentially there may be exceptional humanitarian circumstances in this case. I say "potentially" because, of course, we haven't heard all the argument. So if there's anything you would like to add. I should say that we have a representative of the Government of Croatia here. We do not have a representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, although they have been informed and, as I understand it, have said that they would be prepared to ensure the transportation of the accused to and from the airport. No doubt that can be confirmed by the Registry at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We, of course, hadn't seen anything from The Netherlands. We also hadn't seen any documents supporting the medical condition of the defendant's father. Mr. Kovacic tells me this morning that that was forwarded to the Registry, but for whatever reason, we've never seen it. So we remain unable to comment on that. Other than that, on the merits, the matter has, I think, been fully set out in our response, drafted by Mr. Scott who's not here this morning to supplement it himself, but there's nothing I wish to add in any event, save to say this: The witnesses being called this week all concern Cerkez. I understand from Mr. Kovacic that were there to be any question of his client not being present at court this week, he, Mr. Kovacic, would not be in a position to go ahead, that he wouldn't, I think, have instructions to proceed in his client's absence; accordingly, a consequence, for example, of allowing Mr. Cerkez to leave the Tribunal this week might be that the time would be, not wasted, but we would have to find time elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That, of course, is an aspect of the case which we have in mind. If there were to be any such grant of provisional release of a temporary nature, it would be at the weekend or at a time which would mean the minimum loss of court time. We would expect the Defence to cooperate in the matter by allowing or not opposing the trial going on. The accused would have the opportunity, of course, of hearing from counsel what the witness had said, but, no doubt, that's a matter we can explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That sets the thing out fully in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You should see the certificate from the Split hospital. Have you not seen that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has somebody got a copy of the certificate, please? I'm going to show you my copy. There seems to be no other available. Just cast an eye on it. It's the English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand from Mr. Lopez-Terres, who approached the Registry directly, that their policy is not to release medical documents to the Prosecution, and that's the reason we didn't see it. I'm not in a position really at this short notice to comment on that, beyond having the most limited understanding of what is involved, but thank you very much for showing it to me. It's a matter for the Tribunal whether, on that material, they are satisfied that the risk to the father is serious and immediate. If it is, we've set out in our motion the procedural steps that have to be taken, and if the Court is satisfied that all the Rule-required steps are taken, then it's a matter for the judgement of the Tribunal. But it's not one of our duties to oppose, for opposition's sake, once we've drawn your attention to the factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You've carried out anything that you should carry out. As far as conditions are concerned, is there anything that you would like to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I note the document from the State of Croatia. Once in the State of Croatia, matters are, of course, out of the Tribunal's hands, save on the promise of that state. What I did note was that there wasn't going to be 24-hour supervision, but there was a general condition that he would not be allowed to leave a localised area and would only be allowed to talk to certain people; namely, family and friends, as I recall it. How that is to be policed and monitored is not further specified, so that I recall an offer to have his report or reporting to a police station once a day or at such intervals as the Tribunal might demand. In the absence of any knowledge of how the forces in Croatia operate, we can't propose any tighter regime for his supervision and know of no way in which the State of Croatia will be able to sanction themselves his failure to honour the condition to stay within a particular locality and to speak only to a narrow range of people. One of the problems, of course, inevitably, is that the defendant leaving the Tribunal is equipped with information of the case and the witnesses and so on of the type not necessarily available to others, and there's again no way we can police his dissemination of that knowledge and information. Again without seeking to be obstructive or to oppose simply for opposition's sake, if the Tribunal acts on the basis of Croatia's offers to police and control the situation, it must recognise that it is reposing trust in that state, it will have in mind the collateral problems we've had with the state, and I can imagine that the only way the Court can tighten up the control that Croatia might have would be to require further reporting at police stations. Having said that, there comes a time when frequency of reporting becomes really unfair and unreasonable. You can't ask someone to report every hour. We know that there are certain places where they even have tagging systems, and I don't know whether that exists there, and again the Court might or might not regard that as appropriate or excessive. Even if you have someone ringing in every hour, or whatever might be regarded as appropriate, that doesn't actually amount to 24-hour supervision of communications in a way that there can be supervision of communications with somebody in a detention facility; although, of course, having said that, in this detention facility, there is probably some freedom of communication that isn't policed or controlled. But all this is simply to emphasise that even the supervision at its highest level offered by Croatia, reposes in -- or would repose in both the State and in Mr. Cerkez a high level of trust, and the Chamber must have that in mind. I suppose there's one other thing that hadn't been included in the original response, and I don't wish to dwell on this, but there was a passage in the application which referred to the state of evidence and so on about Mr. Cerkez, and the Tribunal won't have overlooked the direct evidence of a killing that has been given and has not been excluded as irrelevant in this case. So this is by no means a case where the evidence is other than very substantial and extremely serious. Those are all matters of detail, and I'm sure you've probably had them all in mind in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the state of the case is concerned, I have not seen a list of witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The list was sent out, I think, on the 5th of August, and subject to two excisions -- well, to the Registry, it was, I think -- and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong -- the 5th of August. The list was sent out of witnesses by the week. Two witnesses have been withdrawn; one won't come, and I can't remember the reason for the other one's being unavailable, and there's been one substitution. But the list was certainly provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've got a list of witnesses to be called, which I have noted as being dated the 5th of August, but there's no mention of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it says the "11th to the 17th of September, 1999" at the top of the first seven names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can be supplied with copies of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got to keep the Chamber informed of the position on witnesses, in light of recent developments, because there have been one or two problems, but we certainly have evidence available for this week, all of it, as I understand from Mr. Kovacic, concerning Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, you've heard what's been said. We have not decided this matter by any manner or means, but we want to have all the matters in mind. We have received the draft of a document -- rather, the original document in which Mr. Cerkez has signed various conditions. If we were going to make any grant of conditional release, he would have to sign a document which would include those conditions, those undertakings which we think are necessary; for instance, not to discuss matters with witnesses, not to have any dealings with witnesses, and not to discuss the case with anybody. Presumably, he would be prepared to sign such an undertaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for giving me the opportunity to comment. Of course he would sign such an undertaking in whatever form it may be. I should like to recall that previously, when we asked for his provisional release, we had suggested certain measures which the Tribunal might apply. Of course, this was simply an attempt to set out some examples, and in that case too, we explicitly said that the defendant would accept any other conditions or measures which the Tribunal might consider appropriate. In connection with this, I should like to comment on what my learned friend, Mr. Nice, has said, and to do so in practical terms, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with this, if I may, by asking you to deal with the matters with which the Chamber is concerned. First of all, there must be no slippage of time in the trial. If there were to be provisional release, it would be over next weekend. Now, how long are you asking for in terms of this visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my idea was that he should spend in Split, at home and in the hospital visiting his father, at least two days. But in practical terms, in view of travelling time, this would mean an absence of four days: One day to travel there and another day to travel back, and two days' stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The difficulties are these: First of all, four days means inevitably that we may lose time for evidence. Now, is there any reason why we cannot hear evidence in his absence, for instance, evidence in chief, if you were given the opportunity to cross-examine after he had returned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is no problem. We will be ready for those witnesses before Cerkez leaves for the cross-examination, and the Defence accepts that he may be absent in the courtroom for those three days, and that is why I was saying if, theoretically, we are talking about a weekend, then he would be losing at a maximum one and a half days of court time, and we agree that that court time of one and a half or two days may be used to meet in his absence. Of course, we would ask the registry to provide the defendant with a video of the proceedings in court, but this is not a condition. We would be able to recount what had happened and explain to him when he returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've obtained a copy of the flights from here to Zagreb. There are apparently flights every day, so it would theoretically be possible for him to fly out one day, have one or two days in Split, and then return. If we were to order that he went on Friday and returned on, say, Sunday or Monday, is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no comment. That is quite feasible, especially the latter possibility; that is, his returning on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber is concerned that he does not breach any of the conditions and that he returns. How can we be satisfied of those matters, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite agree with that, and the accused personally quite agrees with that. All we can do is give our own word, which I think is, after all, the most important, that he will certainly make no breach. Let me also recall the fact that the defendant surrendered voluntarily to the Tribunal before the beginning of the proceedings. Even though the Prosecution has a different opinion, which is not founded on fact, it is a fact that the accused surrendered of his own free will without any pressures of third parties. That was his own personal decision. The trial has started; he wants to see the end of that trial. He believes that he is innocent, and he believes that we are able to prove it, and he does not wish to remain persecuted, suspected of a criminal offence, for the rest of his life, so he wants to be tried. In the course of the preparations for the trial, as you are aware, we always adopted a constructive approach, and our main proposals were to speed up the beginning of trial, so I think it would be quite illogical to expect an about-turn at this stage. There is not a single fact that would point in that direction, coupled with our personal assurances that he has the most sincere intention of carrying out what he needs to do and of returning to the Tribunal as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps two more sentences only, Your Honours. We do not wish to waste your time, but please, try and bear in mind a very practical aspect of this matter regarding the possibility of influencing witnesses or disturbing witnesses in any sense. If this were to be done in the way that you suggested as a possibility, it would consist of a brief visit in Split, of maybe 48 hours or a little longer, to Split and back from Split. In Split, Cerkez lives four or five minutes' walking distance from the hospital where his father has been admitted. He has no wish or desire to move anywhere else except along that route from the house to the hospital and back. A second point in this connection is that you should bear in mind that Split is in a different state than Vitez; it is five hours' drive from Vitez. And according to all information we have, there are no witnesses or victims in Split. There may be someone by chance, because the Bosniaks who feel threatened or jeopardised certainly didn't go to Split, and therefore there is no theoretical chance of him meeting someone on the street. Perhaps, if it would be helpful, we could ask the Tribunal not to publicise the visit; to make it public upon his return. I understand the Prosecution is afraid that a witness may get the wrong message when he reads in the papers that Cerkez has come to Split to visit his father. The witness may come to the conclusion that he has been released. So if this would be helpful, as we haven't told anyone yet that that is what we have applied for -- only Cerkez's father was told yesterday in hospital that there was a possibility of his son coming to visit him, but he has no intention of talking about that. Anyway, his condition is such that he cannot talk about it. So I think this can be withheld from the public, and perhaps that would minimise the fears of the Prosecution, because, as I said, there are no witnesses or victims in Split. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to stand again, but there are just two things, I think, or three things that I perhaps ought to have raised with you, I hope helpfully. As to publicity, of course, this is open session. Any order can be given privately. As further protection, the Court might make an order now, in respect of those listening to these proceedings, that they shouldn't publicise any part of the application that has been made. I haven't looked up your power to do that, but I'm sure that must lie within your power. More significantly, on the question of disruption of the trial, we've had several witnesses who have been heard in chief and then cross-examinations been postponed. Obviously that's always difficult, but I do know, and I'm going to explain to you that the witness coming at the end of this week is one who is going to be very difficult indeed to get back for cross-examination if his evidence isn't concluded this week. I can explain that more fully later. On the same point, at the end of paragraph 10 of our motion, this point is made, that there are no provisions to permit judicial proceedings to continue in the absence of the accused. That, of course, would have -- if that's right, that would have terrible consequences, if, for whatever reason, a defendant leaving -- not really on provisional release, but on these grounds -- were not to return. That problem might be overcome if the Chamber were to obtain, both for the short-term purposes of witnesses on Friday and Monday and generally against all eventualities, a personal undertaking from the defendant in court to you, the Chamber -- and, indeed, it might be helpful to have that in any event -- but a personal undertaking that he consents to the trial continuing in his absence until further notice, only to be given by him in person. That would mean that if, for whatever reason, he was unable to return, the trial could be taken forward. That might be both consistent with his stated position and it might meet the concerns of the Chamber about loss of time, and it might also deal, at least possibly, with our concern in the last line of paragraph 10. Finally, I'm reminded that apparently the security services here in the ICTY are at least theoretically in a position to go to Croatia and be in Croatia during any period in which Cerkez could be there. If the Chamber felt, whatever the reluctance of the security services here to do that might be, if the Chamber felt that could help, then at least they could seek assistance of those personnel. For my part, I can't immediately see what help they could give, but then I'm not in the security business, and they would be better able to advise you than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask the government of Croatia, please, the representative, to assist us. There is a microphone. It might be easier if you came forward and went to the witness -- just the witness stand. First of all, thank you for coming, Mr. Miljenic. Could you give us your full name, as it were, and your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. I'm Orsat Miljenic, counsellor at the Croatian Embassy here in The Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have provided a statement which we have, a statement of the Embassy of the Republic of Croatia, in which at paragraph 4 you set out your undertaking on behalf of the government to take over Mr. Cerkez at the airport, to ensure he remains within the municipality of Split, to surrender his passport, to ensure he has no contact with any witnesses or people other than his relatives and close friends, and to ensure that he reports once a day to the police. Having heard what's been said here, Mr. Miljenic, is there anything you want to add to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, with your permission, I would like to continue in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we drafted this proposal, we also submitted a list which, as you can see, was left open-ended. If you look at point 5, the Republic of Croatia is prepared to guarantee other matters as soon as necessary. This was just an indication, and we just wanted to provide a framework within which we are prepared to operate. There are additional police measures which can vouchsafe some of these things, so if the Chamber considers that additional measures are necessary, and after our consultations with our own police services and agencies, we can give you further clarifications on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Miljenic, you mentioned the fact that your proposal could be studied and expanded. Would the Croatian government make sure that there would be surveillance not only to and from the airport, but throughout the sojourn of the accused? Could he be under police surveillance to make sure that the conditions of his stay are fully respected; that is, that he should have no contact with any other persons except the father of the accused? ORSAT MILJENIC: [Interpretation] In principle, I believe that there are no difficulties there; but with your permission, being part of the diplomatic corps, I have to also consult, and I believe that some of these consultations can be dealt with on an urgent basis, since the whole matter is urgent, or later on, if the Trial Chamber believes that the additional conditions are necessary, and then we can give you an answer as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it should be done immediately; that is, these consultations, to make sure that the surveillance should be permanent as soon as the accused is taken over at the airport until his return, that he should be monitored by the police until he returns to The Hague, and I think by doing so immediately and by providing an answer to the Tribunal as quickly as possible, that would facilitate the ruling of our Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: I believe that this could be dealt with within a matter of five minutes or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Miljenic, perhaps you would deal with that and let us know your answer. If that could be sent via the legal officer to us, as the Judge says, that would assist us. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider this application and we will submit our decision in due course. The discussion was one which, had an application been made, may well have been heard in a closed session; accordingly, we instruct those in the public gallery who are listening to this not to publicise any details about this application or anything that was said and to regard the matter as if it were in a closed session. Are there any other matters before we go on to the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I think perhaps just one or two. Indeed, on the topic of evidence, Ms. Verhaag corrects me, having researched her records, the list that you were provided on the 5th of August of witnesses didn't have an identification of which ones were being called in the particular week. That was added. As you know, it's my need to get through roughly two witnesses a day if we are to be anywhere near finishing our case before Christmas, and so that leads to an assumption that in any week of five and a half days, there will be nine witnesses. We've actually been told by the Defence since then that they need so much time for cross-examination of the witnesses they want that we've reduced the number. I'll come to the detail of that a little later, but that's the position on the witness list, and I'll come to the detail of the witnesses in just a second or so. My position, just to explain my absences from the court this week and possibly next, is that I'm also running another case in front of Judge Jorda and that Chamber. The Prosecution case ends either at the end of this week or at the beginning of next week, and I have one co-counsel there, so I'm obliged to spend quite a lot of time there. But I'm fortunate in having three co-counsel here, so you'll be seeing more of them and less of me this week, and I hope that's acceptable. I simply notify everyone that the Prosecution expert Ribicic, of whom we've given the name before, should be available in report form by the end of this month or the beginning of October. There are, I think, outstanding, for early disposal, issues about how transcript evidence may be acceptable to the Chamber and what transcript evidence may be accepted and admitted. Can I mention publicly one name that is a name that might be a useful witness to think about as an example? That's the witness Ashdown because he was a public witness when he gave evidence before. There's another, I think in modern terminology, high-profile witness who gave evidence, I think, in closed session on the last time, and I can give his name or identity to the Defence in due course, and the Chamber will know about him. So here are two witnesses, broadly of a similar station and status maybe, and subject to any objections by the Defence, then it will be helpful for us to know how, in general, if the Chamber is going to accept their transcript evidence, it would like to proceed. There was some uncertainty on the last occasion as to whether the evidence had to be read in court or could be read in by being identified. There is the argument on dead and unwilling witnesses, which reached an inconclusive stage on the last occasion. It might be thought useful to have it as something to deal with if, for any reason, we run short of witnesses. If we have that in mind, and if there are oral representations that the Chamber's going to require or any further arguments to be addressed, we can perhaps timetable that in. On the last occasion, the Chamber asked me effectively to review our attitude on providing libraries of documents to the defendants. The Court will remember that there was the reference to Ministry of Defence documents coming from the Cheshire Regiment and so on, and there were other documents which we might have in library form. I think I explained then, but I certainly can explain now that we don't have a library of military documents from the English regiments. Simply, such libraries didn't exist and they don't exist. The documents are attached item by item to particular witness statements, and we have no greater access probably to the material almost than the Defence does, who have applied, through the Ministry of Defence in London, for a range of documents. So that matter, I think, will have to be put, again in the vernacular of the age, on hold. As to ECMM documents, where libraries may exist, I know that there is by them an in-principle opposition to the provision of the library of documents, and so if issue; that is, the provision of documents of that category in bulk, is to be taken forward and if we are to proceed other than by producing particular ECMM documents on a case-by-case basis, I forecast that it may be necessary to schedule a hearing -- am I going too fast? Sorry. It may be necessary to schedule a hearing where ECMM can themselves be represented to make the points and arguments they wish to make on that topic. I mention those issues, both to inform my friends and also to make sure that you don't think we've overlooked what was a hint to us to review the position on providing libraries of documents, which is well in our mind. Finally, and just as a matter of notice at this stage, but so that it shan't be thought to have come as a last-minute thought at a later stage in the case, there's been an Appeals Chamber decision on the four additional witnesses we sought to have added in respect of Zepce, although the decision has been that we cannot have a hearing before the Appeals Chamber. As the Chamber knows, we are in the process of preparing for the village attacks following the dossier decision, and that preparation is fairly well-advanced, I'm happy to say, but the overall change in circumstances about the presentation of evidence in respect of the village victims means that I may, in light of all the circumstances, renew the application for Zepce in respect of the one central witness, and I just give people notice of that. Can I now turn to the state of evidence this week? First, the return of Dr. Allcock. He was the first witness on the list. He was coming back to be cross-examined, following the indication by the Defence that they would require half a day with him. The Chamber may have seen a letter dated September the 9th from Hunter and Williams, in which I gather Mr. Kovacic has now joined, which sets out, as it were, a lawyer's opinion of Dr. Allcock, which followed what may be described as a, I suppose, fairly standard cross-examination on qualifications of certain jurisdictions, and then goes on to say this: "They plan to address the opinions offered," and then they characterise Dr. Allcock in what is a lawyer's opinion or an argumentative opinion, I suppose, "with properly qualified testimony from world-credentialed expert witnesses at the appropriate point in the Defence case." Two things follow from that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't seen this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. It was copied to the Chamber, according to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I can distribute extra copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. If I'd known that, I would have made sure they were available, but it was marked as copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be simplest if Mr. Stein explained the letter to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I can tell you that Dr. Allcock is here, not only because we have observations to make about the propriety of proceeding in this way and the time that will be taken unnecessarily by proceeding in this way, but also because there may be some re-examination and the Chamber may, itself, have questions to ask of him. So he's here and ready, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, perhaps you can enlighten us as to what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Having in mind Your Honours' ruling of 19 March, 1999, rejecting the Prosecution's application that unless questions were specifically put to the witness, the issues raised by the witness's testimony would be deemed waived, having in mind the cross-examination which uncovered Dr. Allcock's expertise or lack thereof, and juxtaposing those qualifications or the lack thereof to the evidence rendered and his opinion, and having in mind the Court's, particularly Judge Robinson's incantation that we need not cross-examine every witness on every thing, we intend to offer no further examination of Dr. Allcock, feeling that it is unnecessary given what I've just said and given that we'll be presenting evidence to challenge his position. We notified the Trial Chamber and the Court so as to alleviate any scheduling difficulties and certainly to let the opposition know that there would be time available today, which had originally been scheduled for Dr. Allcock's presentation. So it is our position to ask no further questions relative to this particular matter, which we forecast by letter and which Mr. Sayers told specifically by telephone to Mr. Scott prior to the letter's submission. We do have -- sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just remind us, if you would: There was some cross-examination then of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, we examined Dr. Alcock, if you recall, on his Ph.D., the title of that Ph.D.; we found out it was about tourism. We cross-examined him relative to his masters' thesis, that being done in, I believe, 1967, and that was on the subject of nuclear power protests in Canada. We talked in great length about the kinds of things that sociologists study and on which they render opinions, and Judge Bennouna correctly opined and examined that this particular witness was a generalist, not a specialist. There was some cross-examination relative to one of the conclusions that an order in December relative to displays of religious artifacts might be offensive. The cross-examination discussed that the display order was at Christmastime and relative to Christmas ornaments. Having studied the transcript, and when Your Honours review it, I think you'll find that the lack of qualifications of Dr. Allcock, particularly when juxtaposed to the wide range of specific opinions on specific issues, that they are certainly of a political science nature, of a history nature, of a linguistic nature, go well beyond the expertise that the witness brings to the Tribunal as an expert on tourism and the sociology of tourism and on nuclear power protests in the late '60s in Canada. With regard to the dead, unavailable witnesses, and Mr. Ribicic specifically, Mr. Sayers would like to address the Tribunal very briefly. We have some papers to file so that when the issues become joined, all the papers will be on deck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should have said that we will deal with those arguments when we can find a convenient time to do so. Any papers that anyone wants to file can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is very unsatisfactory. The position taken by the Defence represents, I suppose, old-fashioned combative practice. Whatever the precise terms of the ruling made in March of this year were, the ruling has been significantly modulated by the Chamber regularly enough now requiring of the Defence an indication as to what is accepted and what is not accepted, and that has always proved helpful because it narrows the issues down. What concerns us is this: Forget the characterisations of the lawyers, which we can deal with in due course. If they say they have properly qualified testimony from world-credentialed expert witnesses, that means they are not shooting in the dark; they apparently have targets. There are things that the witness has said that they disagree with, that are conclusions to which he should have come and has not come that they show he should reach. As opposed to spending an hour, or whatever it was, engaged in what is a comparatively easy task for traditionally educated specialists of the law, all those who have come to the law with other traditional specialisations; that is, the cross-examination of sociologists is sometimes regarded as fair game but are, in fact, real experts, as opposed to doing that, if time had been spent joining issues, we might have got a lot further. They have an expert or experts, they know what their case is, and it should be raised with this witness. The alternative is going to be extremely extravagant in terms of time and it's not going to be helpful to the Chamber because it will inevitably mean that if and when their experts are called, and, of course, they haven't told us what the names of their witnesses or experts are, although I happen to have an understanding of the name of one of them -- it may be right; it may be wrong -- they haven't told us but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, we are wasting time, precious time, and even if we are meeting after the holidays, we must bear in mind that we are being watched by many institutions, so we mustn't waste time. We could examine this matter procedurally without entering into any lengthy discussions. If I have understood you well, and I am quite awake this morning, Mr. Stein told us that there was no need to cross-examine Dr. Allcock. That is what I understood. Where is the problem then? If the Defence does not see the need, as our colleague, Judge Robinson has said, that they don't need to cross-examine everyone, do you have any comment on that matter? Let's not go back into the history of the proceedings as of last March every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly do have a comment, and it's a comment I've made before and I'll make it again, and I was just coming to it, and it's this: If there are issues to be joined, they are better joined with the witness because the expensive and time-consuming alternative will be another witness will be called in the Defence case, raising topics that haven't been raised with this witness, and I shall seek leave to recall the witness in rebuttal, probably having had him here present to instruct me when the witness is giving evidence, all at a great expense of time and money. A great deal of time and money can be saved by modern procedures which include having cases put. The Chamber will recall that I proposed to the Defence that expert reports should be exchanged for agreement of central issues that might be in agreement and that, indeed, experts can be put together to narrow the issues. All those proposals were rejected. What we're going back to here is an old-fashioned slogging match, to use the vernacular, that simply takes time and money. It's not helpful, and the Chamber, with its powers to regulate examination and cross-examination, could and, in our respectful submission, should give this witness an opportunity, through questions that can be focused, of dealing with the Defence case now, rather than obliging him to come back at my request and at the extension of the timetable later on. Those are our observations on that, and we've put that in writing in one way or another to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Nice, the letter that you have just submitted to us is dated -- were you not aware of the position of the Defence before calling the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before calling the witness? No, not at all. If you mean recalling him today, he has to be recalled today in case the Chamber had any questions to ask of him, and I have some questions in re-examination myself and in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that that witness is present in The Hague just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we have a problem on the side of the Defence, a problem of management of the trial. You can't wait for the witness to come to The Hague to formulate your position. You should have formulated your position before the witness arrived in The Hague. You said that you see no use in cross-examining him, but did you tell us that before, before the witness was brought here, Dr. Allcock was brought here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, we did. Yes, we did. We notified telephonically Mr. Scott on the 7th or 8th of September, and this letter forwarded to the Chamber and copied to you just now was dated September 9 was to avoid the inconvenience of Dr. Allcock reappearing. The Prosecution, in response to our letter, said they were going to bring him no matter what because they wanted to rehabilitate him, which is within their power, or have the Court ask questions. So the issue was raised and I sent it to the Chamber to obviate the need to bring him back. While I'm on my feet, this issue has been batted around. Mr. Nice has consistently wanted the old-fashioned and unused by anyone on our team, British rule, relative to if you don't put something to a witness, you waive. Now, with all respect to my colleague, to the British courts, that's a system I'm not familiar with. As we have thought through it, however, it elongates and doesn't save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On that point, I disagree entirely. The point is that we have to decide an issue, and issues of fact -- this may not be a good example and you may be right here -- but where there are issues of fact to be decided, then the purpose is that the witness should be able to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he'd said, for instance, Mr. Kordic was at a meeting and said something incriminating, and the Defence case is that he wasn't there at all, then the witness should have the opportunity of dealing it because he may have some reason for saying that he remembers Mr. Kordic being there. I give that as an example. But that aside, I don't think we need trouble you any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we shall not require any further cross-examination. As has been observed before, this is a Tribunal of professional judges. It must be doubtful as to how much we are going to be assisted in resolving the case by hearing a great deal of cross-examination of experts. Even if there are clashes of opinion, we do not think we will be assisted by cross-examination, at length or otherwise, in these circumstances. But, Mr. Nice, you are quite entitled, of course, to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I have some re-examination of him, and I will ask him to come in in just a second. Before I do, a word to put you in the picture about other witnesses, may we go into private session, for safety, as I deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: adjourned at 10.46 a.m. sine die 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
